1:
Matthew Henry opens by setting the chapter against an older book: the question where wisdom shall be found was asked long before this, and answered only in general, that God knows the place of it; here the teacher goes further and tells us both where we may find it and how we may get it. He then breaks the means into five, that we must be convinced the words of God are the fountain and standard of wisdom, receive them with readiness of mind, hide them as we hide treasure we are afraid of being robbed of, incline our ear to them, and apply our hearts. Adam Clarke presses the last of these hardest, and turns it into a rule about character: a man who has the rule of his duty only in his Bible and in his head is not likely to be steady or consistent, since his heart is not engaged and his obedience can only be forced or done from a sense of duty, which is not the obedience of a loving child; but the man who has the word in his heart works from his heart. John Wesley and John Gill both take the verb for hiding as laying up a choicest treasure.

The mining figure of the fourth verse is taken literally by two of them, on entirely different evidence. Charles Ellicott argues that the process was understood long before the time this book is ascribed to, proving it from the remains of copper mines found in one peninsula and gold mines in a desert of another country, with rock inscriptions near the first dated by one scholar four thousand years before our era; he adds that the silver of that court came from two distant regions, one of them probably in Spain. Clarke goes instead to his own century and to the other side of the world: in a distant country slaves are employed to scrape the soil from a river bed and wash it for particles of gold and diamonds, and by a law of that state whoever finds a diamond of a certain weight receives his freedom, which produces the greatest ardour and diligence in the searching — so precious, Clarke says, is liberty to the human heart. That is how wisdom is to be sought, and he who succeeds finds the liberty of the children of God and is saved from the slavery of sin. Ellicott explains the second half of the verse from custom: the insecurity of life and property in those countries made the hiding of treasure in the earth frequent, and owners often died without disclosing the place, so that hunting for such hoards has always been of the keenest interest there, and furnishes the ground of one of the Gospel parables. Keil and Delitzsch supply the philology that matches, that the verb for searching comes from the primary meaning of a ditch and is related in its root-idea to a verb meaning to dig.

They also report an old rabbinic direction to read the third verse otherwise than it stands, so that instead of yea if thou criest, the sense becomes if thou callest understanding mother — a reading they set aside, preferring that the seeker calls understanding to himself and invites her. On the promise that follows, Ellicott makes the knowledge of God the highest of all gifts and eternal life itself, yet observes that our knowledge here is so imperfect beside what is to come that an apostle described our relation to God now as better expressed by being known of him than by knowing him. Gill reads the whole chapter christologically, taking wisdom for Christ and the instruction offered for the Gospel, and the fear of the Lord for a grace wrought in the heart rather than a lesson learned.
6:
The stanza begins by taking back what the previous one seemed to give. John Gill notices the shift and states its purpose: the declaration that God gives wisdom is set here partly to caution those who search after it and find it not to attribute the finding to their own diligence and industry but to grace, and partly as a direction where to go for it. Charles Ellicott supplies the parallel from a later writer, that God gives to every man liberally and upbraideth not, and glosses the last word as meaning that he does not blame a man for asking.

The term rendered sound wisdom is the crux of the section, and four senses are offered for it. Gill reports two Jewish commentators making it the law, because it endures when all other beings come to nothing, and rejects that for the Gospel, which is sound doctrine in opposition to a science falsely so called. He then gives the philological sense as essence or substance, that which really is and is solid. Adam Clarke agrees with the last and confesses the difficulty openly: it is hard to find in any language a term proper to express the original meaning, which seems generally to mean the essence or substance of a thing, the thing itself, that which is chief of its kind; so that God lays up for the righteous what is essential. He also quotes an older English version rendering the clause that God preserves the welfare of the righteous. Ellicott takes the opposite line entirely, rendering the word literally as furtherance or advancement, and comparing the saying that to whoever has, more shall be given.

Who is kept in the following verse is likewise unsettled. Gill notes that the words may be rendered as an infinitive, to keep the paths of judgment, so that the clause states the effect of God’s being a buckler rather than a separate act of his; Ellicott takes the plain sense that God protects those who walk in those paths; John Wesley allows that keeping paths may stand for keeping men in their paths. On the noun rendered saints in the same verse Ellicott supplies an unusually full history: the word means rather God’s ardent worshippers, is used in the law of the tribe set apart for his service on account of their zeal, occurs very frequently in the Psalter, and by the time of the Maccabees had been taken as a party name by those voluntarily devoted to the law in opposition to men who favoured Greek religion and culture; the English word saint, he adds, rather implies dedication. Clarke closes the section by repeating in another form the rule he laid down at its opening: he who is taught of God understands the whole law of justice, mercy, righteousness and truth, because God has written it on his heart, whereas he who understands these things by books only is never likely to practise or profit by them.
10:
The conjunction that opens this section is changed by two of them. Charles Ellicott holds the verse better taken as an explanation of what precedes, reading for wisdom will enter rather than when wisdom entereth, and Keil and Delitzsch render it the same way, treating the pair of verses as an expansion of the earlier promise that then thou shalt understand. Matthew Henry asks instead when wisdom can be said to have entire possession, and answers with two marks, that it has dominion over us and that we delight in it: it must not merely fill the head with notions but enter the heart and give law to the affections, working there as leaven in dough, to diffuse its relish and change the mass into its own image. This is the third place in the chapter where the heart is set against the head, after Adam Clarke on hiding the words and again on being taught of God rather than out of books; and Henry adds a test, that the tree will be known by its fruits, so that if we are truly wise it will appear in our care to avoid evil company and evil practices.

The word rendered discretion is one that can go either way, and Clarke says so: here it is taken in a good sense, of a good device, so that the man invents purposes of good and all his schemes have God’s glory and the good of others for their object. But Clarke prefers an older English rendering to the received one outright, quoting a version that gives then shall counsel preserve thee and calling it a very good translation, much better than the present. John Gill arrives independently at the same word, reporting that the Greek version renders it good counsel, and he offers a second possibility of his own, that the clause means discretion will watch over thee.

On the man who speaks froward things they divide between a liar and an agitator. Ellicott renders the noun misrepresentations and distortions of the truth, and Keil and Delitzsch the same, misrepresentations of the good and the true for the purpose of deceiving. Clarke derives it instead from a verb meaning to turn or change the course of a thing, and makes it things of subversion, so that the men described are those who wish to subvert the state of things whether civil or religious, being seditious themselves and wishing to make others so — men, he adds, who speak much of liberty and oppression, deal greatly in broad assertions, and endeavour especially to corrupt the minds of youth. Gill notices what is implied by the next verse’s word for leaving: it supposes these men to have been externally in the right ways, having had a religious education, and though people do not easily leave the ways they were brought up in, there are instances of it, and such are generally the worst of men. On the delight in evil that follows, Ellicott observes that this positive taking of pleasure in it is named by an apostle as the last stage of degradation, and Keil and Delitzsch quote a commentator to the effect that the perversities meant are not simple or common ones but the worst and vicious in every part. John Wesley reduces the crooked ways of the closing verse to men who swerve from the straight way and have windings and turnings by which to escape conviction.
16:
Two adjectives describe the woman, and what they mean divides the chapter’s readers. Charles Ellicott holds that the first implies she belonged to another family and the second to another nation, and builds a small social history on it: the example of the king to whom this book is ascribed, in marrying foreign wives, seems to have become common, and such women, brought up in the lax morality then prevailing among the neighbouring peoples, would not consider themselves bound by the high standard of purity the law enjoined on their new countrywomen. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same distinction by philology and support it independently, the first word meaning simply what does not belong to me and the second scarcely ever losing the mark of foreign origin; and they add that prostitution was partly sanctioned in the worship of several neighbouring nations and there regarded as nothing less than customary, whereas the law forbade it. John Gill denies the national sense flatly, holding her called strange not because she is of another nation or unknown but because she belongs to another man. Gill then reports three allegorical readings, of the sensitive appetite, of idolatry, and of false doctrine generally, and applies the passage himself to the corruptions of a church; Keil and Delitzsch explain why such readings arose, since the language of the prophets about apostasy suggested to the old interpreters that the adulteress personifies apostasy or heresy.

Who the guide of her youth is has four answers. Gill canvasses God, her parent and her husband, and settles on the husband, noting the word may be rendered the friend or companion of her youth; Ellicott says the same, that it is rather the friend with whom she has lived in intimacy, in other words her first love; Keil and Delitzsch derive the noun from a verb meaning to accustom oneself to a person and make it the familiar associate. Adam Clarke alone takes the parent, so that she leaves her father’s house and instructions. On the covenant Clarke offers both renouncing the true religion and the matrimonial contract, while Ellicott and John Wesley keep only the second, Wesley noting it is called God’s because he is the author of the obligation and is called to witness it. Clarke supplies an etymology for the flattering of the next clause, that the word means smoothing with words and intimates glib and oily speech, and claims that an English verb is derived from it.

The verse about the house is construed three ways. Gill gives the received sense, that the house inclines to death, and a second in which she inclines to death, which is her house, on the authority of two Jewish commentators and an Aramaic paraphrase; Ellicott renders it that she sinks down with her house, house and all, like the men the earth swallowed; Keil and Delitzsch report the Greek version as saying she placed her house beside death, and suspect it may be the original, the received text being doubtful. Clarke reads it topographically instead, that such houses are established in by and secret places off the high road, so that every step toward one is a step toward death. He then turns to his own century at the following verse. Very few such women, he says, ever return to sobriety, and perhaps none of those who came to it by inclination; among those who were deceived and abandoned many have been reclaimed, and to those alone the reformatory houses of his day may be useful, while to the others they may be only incentives to further sinning. Gill records that some of the ancients thought this sin unpardonable, and answers that some have certainly been recovered, though the Aramaic version adds that they do not return in peace.
